newsitem.title: JAPAN: 'Rest' goal of first Japanese hostage to come home.
newsitem.headline: 'Rest' goal of first Japanese hostage to come home.

text.p: The first Japanese hostage to return home after being rescued from Marxist rebels in Lima said on Friday that after a traumatic four months in captivity all he wanted to do was rest at home.

"The first thing I want to do is go home, stretch and get some rest," said Shigeru Taki, one of 24 Japanese among 71 hostages rescued on Wednesday in the fiery military strike which ended an 18-week siege at the Japanese ambassador's home.

Taki, 59, president of National Peruana S.A., Matsushita Electric Industrial Co's Peru branch, arrived at Kansai International Airport in the central commercial city of Osaka shortly after 6 p.m (0900 gmt).

The silver-haired businessman, who sat in a wheelchair flanked by his wife Tetsuyo, two tearful daughters and a Matsushita executive, sprained his ankle during the dramatic hostage rescue, but said he was able to walk unaided.
He was scheduled to go to a local hospital for a check-up before returning home with his family.
His wife Tetsuyo, 60, said she watched the raid on the diplomatic compound by crack Peruvian troops on television.
"When I saw the smoke rise from the building as the assault started, I thought I'd never see my husband again," she told an airport news conference.
"Support expressed in letters from friends, family, and loved ones sustained me," Taki said of his 126 days as a prisoner of the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
"The toughest thing to face was two fears: that the Peruvian army would raid and that the MRTA would, at some point, torture hostages," he said.
He said there were occasional scuffles between captors and hostages and occasions when the guerrillas struck hostages who had defied orders, but no arbitrary beatings or torture.
Days began with 60 minutes of exercise and were followed by marathon games of chess, Japanese and Chinese board games and Japanese and Spanish language lessons, he said.
Taki, one of Matsushita's Latin America experts and a veteran of more than a decade in the region, said he would return to Peru after a brief vacation.

Psychotherapist Naho Kikuchi warned the legacy of 126 days confinement inside the residence, living with the fear of imminent death, will plague some hostages with phantom aches and pains and recurring fears triggered by chance events.

"The symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are they will feel psychologically stressed without knowing the reason why. For example, on an anniversary date two years from now, they may have a stomach ache and that is a physical sign saying they have to deal with their emotional problem," she told Reuters.
